interactions.summary: Carol reads Piccarda's story: she took vows, was violently pulled from the cloister, and kept the veil on her heart even after being forced back into worldly life; Constance is named as another such figure.

Jiang paraphrases the scene as a case of family power politics: Piccarda wanted God, her powerful brother needed her marriage for alliance-building, and although her body was taken back into worldly marriage, her heart stayed loyal to God. He then sharpens the paradox that these apparently innocent women still occupy the lowest sphere.

Students propose that the women lacked enough ambition or free-willed resistance, while Jiang presses how resistance would have been possible under armed coercion until another student notes that suicide is blocked by Catholic teaching.

speaker_notes.note: Jiang's paraphrase is noisy and compresses names and family relations, but the stable structure is clear: coerced removal from religious vows for dynastic marriage, with interior fidelity to God surviving bodily violation.

claims.claim: Piccarda says she entered a religious order young, was violently taken from the cloister, and kept the veil in her heart even after being turned back to the world against her will.
Jiang interprets Piccarda's story as one where family power politics used her as a marriage pawn even though she wanted to devote herself to God.
Jiang argues that the women appear to have done nothing wrong, yet their presence in the lowest sphere implies that Dante's heaven still registers some deficiency in their response.
A student proposes that the women failed by not exercising enough free will or ambition to resist what was done to them.
Jiang tests that proposal by asking how resistance was possible under armed coercion, prompting the classroom toward the constraint that suicide itself would count as sin.

signature_moments.moment: Piccarda's body is dragged back into the world, but the veil on her heart never comes off.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the veil upon her heart was never loosed
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves Dante's sharp distinction between outward coercion and inward fidelity, which becomes the basis of Jiang's paradox.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang forces the contradiction: they did nothing wrong, yet God still leaves them in the lowest sphere.
signature_moments.source_phrase: they did everything right they did nothing wrong yet at the same time they are in the lowest sphere
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's central moral pressure point and sets up the next discussion about suicide, coercion, and what counts as real free will.

signature_moments.moment: The only obvious forms of resistance Jiang can name are escape or death, which reveals how severe the bind really is.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there are soldiers with swords dragging her away what could she have done
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It shows Jiang refusing an easy moralism about free will by making the coercive scene concrete.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Dante's image for inward fidelity to religious vows surviving outward force and worldly marriage.
Jiang's shorthand for the dynastic alliance logic that reclaims Piccarda from the convent and treats her as political leverage.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture moves from the abstract paradox of heavenly hierarchy into a concrete biography of coerced vows. Jiang uses Piccarda and Constance to test how paradise judges outward force, inward fidelity, and the limits of resistance.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang's rapid paraphrase contains noisy ASR around names and familial roles. Keep the durable structure of coerced marriage and persistent inner loyalty rather than overcommitting to exact kinship wording from this packet alone.
